"No successful PHP2Shell exploits seen so far"... in the wild, specifically in Wiz's honeypot. The vulnerability itself has been successfully exploited, most notably for the "Steal my Bitcoin" challenge [1] as one example.

Dan Guido, of Trail of Bits, claims they have an "universal" exploit [2]. Knowing their track record, I don't currently have a reason to doubt this claim.

[1]: https://stealmybitcoin.com/

[2]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50226010

EDIT: The HN title has been changed since posting this comment.

It's funny that when stealmybitcoin.com was posted on HN (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50224916) there were hundreds of top voted comments saying "see no one has been able to steal it, the reported vulnerability was fake, it's all AI marketing" etc.

Since it was successfully exploited there has been zero further discussion, and I bet most people who participated in the original thread aren't even aware.

As one of those comments I dispute your characterization of it as the reported vulnerability being fake, very few people were saying that. The main thing being called fake was the narrative that with AI it was trivial to exploit the vulnerability.

It has not escaped me that the successful exploit did in fact just say “codex, exploit this” and got it.

I had assumed the rash of commenters saying “lol I am not revealing my AI’s exploit for a measly 500 bucks” were saying that because their AI attempt failed. Now I know they didn’t even try!

If you follow the threads, it looks like the original post wasn’t exploitable. It looks like it was hacked within an hour of being made exploitable (actually running php).

> The failed leaks highlight a broader challenge: building a generalized exploit that works reliably across PHP versions and deployment configurations is difficult. As far as I know, there has been no proven vulnerability on a modern PHP (production) stack. The "Steal my Bitcoin" challenge was a toy project. The "lab" target used the embedded PHP server (`php -S`) which is for development only.

> Warning. This web server is designed to aid application development. [...] It should not be used on a public network. https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.commandline.webserver...

There are 3 main PHP interfaces (SAPI):

1. mod_php which is obsolete and requires Apache prefork (which should also be avoided)

2. php-fpm (FastCGI) which has been the default for more than a decade.

3. FrankenPHP is a new official interface much more suitable for containers.

There were 2 vulnerabilities.:

1. "OOM corruption". The advisory says there was a proven exploit with mod_php, but only for that obsolete SAPI. "Source analysis therefore supports FPM as a susceptible, though *no complete FPM exploit* has been demonstrated for this SAPI."

2. "stale global state". The advisory is The last PHP release (8.5) was vulnerable when the debug parameter fatal_error_backtraces was on. There was a suspicion that an exploit could exist in the session code for php-fpm, but it was unproven and probably unrealistic.

The "evidence" given at the end of the article seems old news to me. The honeypot was based on Apache-prefork + mod_php. As stated in the CVE, there is a proven exploit for that (obsolete) stack.

For teams still working through the patching, the practical first step is an inventory of which internet-facing hosts and containers actually run an affected PHP version, since that list is often incomplete. Patching also does not remove anything already planted, so on exposed hosts it is worth checking web roots and upload directories for new or modified PHP files and reviewing access logs from before the patch date. Honeypot data showing few successful attempts is a useful trend signal, but it says little about whether your own servers were hit.

It is an old, bad language and interpreter, so it's widely used and lacks an investment of money, effort and talent. Perfect target for exploitation.

Php is still under active development, and has seen a lot of architectural changes at the language level over the last decade that have seen real benefits.

Now, imho, it still isn't a good language, but I wouldn't call it "old". It's not COBOL or FORTRAN where the people who wrote a lot of the mission-critical stuff that banks, research labs, hospitals, and government rely on died 20+ years ago.

A lot of it not receiving investment doesn't come at the language project level, but the individual project level. Accounting likes to pretend that the maintenance portion of the SDLC doesn't exist past a certain point because "what about the shareholders!?" and there are, to date, very few incentives for them to look at the problem in any other way. Let's say you run a Php application that's got Php2Shell vulns and you want to patch it but the only way to do that is to shift major versions, meaning a rewrite of some or all of the code. The code "works fine" according to the bean counters, and there's nothing saying they'll get fined or jailed if a breach occurs as a result, so your project doesn't get funded.

Php was at the forefront of dynamic websites. Early versions also harbored a lot of security vulnerabilities. Php catered to shit browsers in the early 00s. Every single company I have worked with that depended on PHP has been focused on non-technical excellence. It's a bad language. Getting good at using it is a waste, in any state it's been in for 20+ years. Making it work is about appeasing your business overlords and leaving better things off the table.
